messages.author: Aurélie Brunet
messages.content:
Hi all! I'm Aurélie, I make kitchen and dining furniture in a two-person workshop near Nantes. Twelve years a cabinetmaker, three on my own. Mostly oak and ash, some walnut when a client can afford it. I joined because I'm about to price my first big commission alone and I'd love a second opinion before I send the quote.

📍 Nantes, FR

messages.author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
messages.content:
Hello everyone, Tomasz here. Joiner by trade, I do staircases and window frames for renovation jobs, and I've just started building small tables in the evenings to see if there's a market. Happy to answer anything about stairs, less happy about finishing, which I'm bad at 😅

📍 Bristol, UK

messages.author: Nadia Haddad
messages.content:
Bonjour! I teach woodworking to adults (evening classes, 8 students at a time) and I build chairs. Steam-bending is my thing. Looking for people to swap offcuts with and for ideas on how to keep beginners safe on the bandsaw.

📍 Montréal, QC

messages.author: Olumide Adeyemi

messages.author: Hugo Martel
messages.content: First commission from the market stall: a set of six oak stools for a bakery café. Simple, but the owner wanted them to stack, which made the leg splay a puzzle.

messages.author: Nadia Haddad

messages.author: Priya Raman
messages.content: Work in progress: cherry writing desk, drawer boxes glued up today. Hand-cut half-blind dovetails on the fronts, machine on the backs, and I'm not ashamed of it.

messages.author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
messages.content: Question for the table makers: gluing up a 90 cm wide oak top from five boards, how many clamps do you use and do you alternate them top and bottom? My last one cupped a little after a week.

messages.author: Karin Lindqvist
messages.content:
Clamp every 20 to 25 cm, alternating above and below, and cauls across the ends. But a cup after a week is usually moisture, not clamping: were the boards at the same moisture before you glued?

In reply to Tomasz Wierzbicki's message:
Gluing up a 90 cm wide oak top from five boards, how many clamps do you use?

messages.author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
messages.content:
Honestly I didn't check. They'd been in the workshop for a week, I thought that was enough.

In reply to Karin Lindqvist's message:
Were the boards at the same moisture before you glued?

messages.author: Samuel Okafor
messages.content: A week is not enough in autumn. I leave boards at least three weeks in the workshop, stickered, and I check with a moisture meter: I want them all within 1 percent of each other and between 8 and 10 percent for indoor furniture.

messages.author: Priya Raman
messages.content: Also worth alternating the growth rings if you're not bookmatching for looks. Doesn't stop movement but it keeps a cup from adding up across the top.

messages.author: Olumide Adeyemi
messages.content: Someone at the workshop told me to drawbore the mortise and tenon joints on my graduation bench instead of relying on glue. How far do you offset the peg hole? I've read everything from 1 mm to 3 mm.

messages.author: Hugo Martel
messages.content:
About 1.5 mm in oak for a 10 mm peg. More than 2 mm and you risk splitting the tenon cheek or snapping the peg on the way in. Make a test joint first with offcuts of the same board.

In reply to Olumide Adeyemi's message:
How far do you offset the peg hole?

messages.author: Aurélie Brunet
messages.content: My workshop is at 12°C these days and hardwax oil is taking forever: three days and still tacky on the underside of a table. Is it the cold or am I putting too much on?

messages.author: Karin Lindqvist
messages.content:
Both, probably. Oils cure slowly below 15°C. Wipe the excess off hard after 20 minutes, one very thin coat, and bring the piece into a warmer room to cure if you can. Tacky after three days usually means oil left sitting on the surface.

In reply to Aurélie Brunet's message:
Three days and still tacky on the underside of a table.

messages.author: Nadia Haddad
messages.content: In winter I switch to shellac for small pieces because it doesn't care about the temperature. Not for a dining table though, it hates water and heat.

messages.author: Aurélie Brunet
messages.content: Wiped it back hard and moved it into the house. Dry by the next morning. Thank you!

messages.author: Olumide Adeyemi
messages.content: What angle do you sharpen bench chisels at? My tutor says 25 degrees, the workshop owner says 30 and they both look at me like the other one is wrong.

messages.author: Samuel Okafor
messages.content:
25 primary and a 30 microbevel works for most of us. Go steeper for chopping hardwood mortises, shallower for paring softwood. They're both right, which is why they both look at you like that.

In reply to Olumide Adeyemi's message:
What angle do you sharpen bench chisels at?

messages.author: Hugo Martel
messages.content: Anyone else stopped using a honing guide? I did a month ago and my edges are rounder than before. Going back to the guide, pride can wait.

messages.author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
messages.content: Selling my old 250 mm table saw blade collection, eight blades, most of them still sharp, because I've switched to a track saw for sheet goods. Free to anyone in the Bristol hub who can collect.

messages.author: Aurélie Brunet
messages.content: Here's the job I mentioned: a solid oak extending dining table, 180 cm extending to 240 cm, for a family of six. My costs: 1,150 euros of timber and hardware, and I estimate 70 hours. I was going to quote 4,800 euros. Too low? Too high?

messages.author: Karin Lindqvist
messages.content:
Work out your real hourly rate first: workshop rent, insurance, machine wear, unpaid time on quotes and admin. Most of us who did that found we needed 55 to 65 euros an hour to stay in business. At 70 hours that's already above your quote before timber.

In reply to Aurélie Brunet's message:
I was going to quote 4,800 euros. Too low? Too high?

messages.author: Hugo Martel
messages.content: And put the extension mechanism in as its own line. Clients understand that a mechanism costs money; they don't understand hours.

messages.author: Priya Raman
messages.content: I charge design time separately now: two drawings and one revision included, anything after that at the hourly rate. Since I started, clients decide faster and I stopped drawing tables nobody buys.

messages.author: Aurélie Brunet
messages.content:
Recalculated with a proper rate: 5,900 euros, with design included and the mechanism on its own line. Sending it tomorrow. Terrifying.

In reply to Karin Lindqvist's message:
Most of us who did that found we needed 55 to 65 euros an hour to stay in business.
